exercises.title: Evaluating a linear spline
exercises.description: Determine the linear spline through $(0,1)$, $(2,5)$, $(4,3)$ and evaluate it at $x = 1$ and $x = 3$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
On each subinterval the line through its two end points.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
The polygon has a kink at $x = 2$ (slope jumps from $2$ to $-1$) – only $C^0$.

exercises.title: Counting conditions
exercises.description: A cubic spline has $n = 4$ subintervals. How many coefficients are there, how many interpolation and smoothness conditions, how many boundary conditions are missing?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$4$ coefficients per subinterval.

Step 2: Unknowns
$4n = 16$ coefficients.

Step 3: Conditions
Interpolation: $2n = 8$. $C^1$ at $3$ interior nodes: $3$. $C^2$: $3$. Together $14$.

Step 4: Difference
$16 - 14 = 2$ missing conditions: boundary conditions (natural, clamped, periodic, not-a-knot).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
In general: $4n - (4n - 2) = 2$, independent of $n$.

exercises.title: Checking C⁰, C¹, C²
exercises.description: Is $s(x) = x^2$ for $0 \le x \le 1$ and $s(x) = 2x - 1$ for $1 \le x \le 2$ continuous, $C^1$, $C^2$?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Compare value, first and second derivative at the node $x = 1$ from left and right.

Step 2: Value
Left $1^2 = 1$, right $2 - 1 = 1$ ✓ continuous.

Step 3: First derivative
Left $2x = 2$, right $2$ ✓ $C^1$.

Step 4: Second derivative
Left $2$, right $0$ ✗: jump of $2$. So $C^1$ but not $C^2$ – not a cubic spline (but a quadratic one).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Always compare all derivatives up to the required order at the node.

exercises.title: Natural boundary condition
exercises.description: State the natural boundary condition for a cubic spline with nodes $x_0 < \dots < x_n$ and explain what it means geometrically.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
It concerns the second derivative (curvature) at the ends.

Step 2: Condition
$s''(x_0) = 0$ and $s''(x_n) = 0$, i.e. $M_0 = M_n = 0$.

Step 3: Meaning
The curvature vanishes at the ends: the curve runs out in a straight line – the wooden strip is not clamped there but free.

Step 4: Consequence
Only $n - 1$ moments $M_1, \dots, M_{n-1}$ are unknown: a tridiagonal $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ system.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
“Natural” means: no additional information about the derivatives – convenient but less accurate near the boundary.

exercises.title: Estimating the polygon error
exercises.description: Estimate the maximal error of the linear spline for $f(x) = \sin x$ on $[0,1]$ with $h = 0.25$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Bound: $\frac{h^2}{8}\max|f''|$.

Step 3: Comparison
The true maximal error is $0.0060$ (near the end of the interval where $|f''|$ is largest) – below the bound ✓.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Half the step ⇒ error bound $/4$.

exercises.title: Is the function a spline?
exercises.description: Decide whether $s(x) = x^3$ ($0 \le x \le 1$), $s(x) = 3x^2 - 3x + 1$ ($1 \le x \le 2$) is a cubic spline.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Degree $\le 3$ per piece and $C^2$ at the node $x = 1$.

Step 4: Result
Yes: a cubic spline (the second function is even only quadratic – the degree may be lower). The third derivative jumps from $6$ to $0$ – that is allowed.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Cubic means “degree at most 3”. $C^3$ is not required – $s'''$ may jump there.

exercises.title: Reading moments off s''
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$M_i = s''(x_i)$.

Step 2: Second derivatives
$s_0'' = -3x$, $s_1'' = -3 + 3(x - 1)$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
$M_0 = M_2 = 0$: it is a natural spline. $s''$ is piecewise linear and continuous.

exercises.title: Checking smoothness at a node
exercises.description: For $s_0 = 1.5x - 0.5x^3$ ($[0,1]$) and $s_1 = 1 - 1.5(x-1)^2 + 0.5(x-1)^3$ ($[1,2]$) check value, first and second derivative at $x = 1$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
From the left $s_0$ at $x = 1$, from the right $s_1$ at $t = x - 1 = 0$.

Step 4: Curvature
$s_0''(1) = -3$, $s_1''(1) = -3$ ✓. Third derivative: $s_0''' = -3$, $s_1''' = 3$ – jumps, allowed.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The seam between two polynomial pieces is invisible up to the second derivative.

exercises.title: Natural spline through 3 points
exercises.description: Determine the natural cubic spline through $(0,1), (1,0), (2,3)$ ($h = 1$) completely.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
One interior moment $M_1$ from the moment equation, then both pieces.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Check all conditions (value, $s'$, $s''$ at the nodes) in exam problems as well.

exercises.title: Natural spline through 4 points
exercises.description: Compute the moments of the natural spline through $(0,0), (1,1), (2,0), (3,1)$ and evaluate it at $x = 0.5$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$M_0 = M_3 = 0$; two equations for $M_1, M_2$.

Step 3: Solution
$M_2 = -12 - 4M_1$ into the second: $M_1 - 48 - 16M_1 = 12 \Rightarrow M_1 = -4$, $M_2 = 4$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
For comparison: the cubic interpolation polynomial has the value $1.0$ at $0.5$ – the spline stays between the data.

exercises.title: Clamped spline through 3 points
exercises.description: Determine the clamped spline through $(0,0), (1,1), (2,0)$ with $s'(0) = s'(2) = 0$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Three moments $M_0, M_1, M_2$: boundary equations plus one interior.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Horizontal tangents at $0$, $1$, $2$. Compared with the natural spline ($M_1 = -3$) the curvature is much stronger.

exercises.title: Piece from moments
exercises.description: On the interval $[0,2]$ ($h = 2$) let $y_0 = 2$, $y_1 = 3$, $M_0 = 0$, $M_1 = -6$. Set up the piece $s(x)$ and check $s(2) = 3$, $s''(2) = -6$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$s(x) = y_0 + bt + \frac{M_0}{2}t^2 + \frac{M_1 - M_0}{6h}t^3$ with $b = \frac{y_1 - y_0}{h} - \frac{h(2M_0 + M_1)}{6}$.

Step 2: Coefficients
$b = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{2(0 - 6)}{6} = 0.5 + 2 = 2.5$. Cubic term: $\frac{-6 - 0}{6\cdot2} = -0.5$.

Step 3: Polynomial
$s(x) = 2 + 2.5x - 0.5x^3$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Do not mix up the formula with $t = x - x_i$ and the denominator $6h$ before the cubic term.

exercises.title: Evaluating a spline at an intermediate point
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
First choose the right subinterval.

Step 4: Plausibility
Both values lie between $0$ and $1$ and between the neighbouring data, fitting the smooth course. For comparison the polygon: $0.5$ and $0.75$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Determine the subinterval, form $t = x - x_i$, insert into the piece.

exercises.title: Thomas algorithm (5 points)
exercises.description: Compute the moments of the natural spline through $(0,0), (1,1), (2,0), (3,1), (4,0)$ with the Thomas algorithm (system $\mathrm{tridiag}(1,4,1)M = (-12, 12, -12)^T$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Forward elimination, then back substitution (4.3).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Symmetric data ⇒ symmetric moments ($M_1 = M_3$). $O(n)$ cost.

exercises.title: Quadratic spline: conditions
exercises.description: For a quadratic spline ($C^1$) with $n$ subintervals count the unknowns and conditions. How many boundary conditions are missing?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Degree $2$: $3$ coefficients per interval.

Step 2: Unknowns
$3n$.

Step 3: Conditions
Interpolation $2n$, $C^1$ at $n - 1$ nodes: $n - 1$. Together $3n - 1$.

Step 4: Missing
$3n - (3n - 1) = 1$ missing condition (e.g. $s'(x_0) = y_0'$) – the spline is asymmetric with respect to the ends.

Step 5: Comparison
Cubic has $2$ missing conditions – symmetric (one per end). That is why cubic splines are the standard.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
In general: degree $k$, smoothness $C^{k-1}$: $k - 1$ missing conditions.

exercises.title: Spline versus interpolation polynomial
exercises.description: For $f(x) = \frac{1}{1 + 25x^2}$ on $[-1,1]$ with $11$ equidistant nodes the maximal error of the interpolation polynomial is $1.92$, that of the natural cubic spline $0.022$. Explain this and judge what happens with $21$ nodes (polynomial $60$, spline $0.0032$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Compare how the error depends on $n$.

Step 2: Polynomial
Error $\propto \frac{f^{(n+1)}}{(n+1)!}\omega(x)$ grows with $n$ because of the large derivatives of $f$: $1.92 \to 60$ (Runge, 4.9).

Step 3: Spline
Error $\propto h^4\|f^{(4)}\|$ decreases with $h$: from $h = 0.2$ to $h = 0.1$ by a factor of $\approx 7$ ($0.022 \to 0.0032$; the factor $16$ holds asymptotically, here the boundary and the large derivative interfere).

Step 4: Conclusion
More nodes always improve the spline, but not the polynomial for equidistant nodes. Splines use local information: a node influences only its neighbourhood (exponentially decaying).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
For many data points: splines instead of high polynomial degrees.

exercises.title: Deriving the moment equations
exercises.description: Derive from the continuity of $s'$ at $x_i$ the equation $M_{i-1} + 4M_i + M_{i+1} = \frac{6}{h^2}(y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1})$ (equidistant, $h$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Equate the derivatives of the pieces at the node from left and right.

Step 2: Slopes
$s_i'(x_i) = b_i = \frac{y_{i+1} - y_i}{h} - \frac{h(2M_i + M_{i+1})}{6}$. From the left: $s_{i-1}'(x_i) = b_{i-1} + M_{i-1}h + \frac{M_i - M_{i-1}}{2h}h^2 = b_{i-1} + \frac{h}{2}(M_{i-1} + M_i)$.

Step 3: Plugging in
$b_{i-1} + \frac h2(M_{i-1} + M_i) = \frac{y_i - y_{i-1}}{h} - \frac{h(2M_{i-1} + M_i)}{6} + \frac h2(M_{i-1} + M_i) = \frac{y_i - y_{i-1}}{h} + \frac h6M_{i-1} + \frac h3M_i$.

Step 4: Equating
With $b_i = \frac{y_{i+1} - y_i}{h} - \frac h3M_i - \frac h6M_{i+1}$: $\frac{y_i - y_{i-1}}{h} + \frac h6M_{i-1} + \frac h3M_i = \frac{y_{i+1} - y_i}{h} - \frac h3M_i - \frac h6M_{i+1}$.

Step 5: Result
Multiplying by $\frac6h$: $M_{i-1} + 4M_i + M_{i+1} = \frac{6}{h^2}(y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1})$ ✓.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
The structure (1, 4, 1) comes from the weights $\frac h6, \frac{2h}{3}, \frac h6$ – Simpson weights!

exercises.title: Proving the minimality property
exercises.description: Let $s$ be the natural cubic spline and $g \in C^2[a,b]$ with $g(x_i) = s(x_i) = y_i$. Show $\int(s'')^2 \le \int(g'')^2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Write $g'' = s'' + e''$ with $e = g - s$ and show that the mixed term vanishes.

Step 2: Splitting
$\int(g'')^2 = \int(s'')^2 + 2\int s''e'' + \int(e'')^2$.

Step 3: Integration by parts
On each $[x_{i-1},x_i]$: $\int s''e'' = [s''e']_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i} - \int s'''e'$. Twice: $= [s''e'] - [s'''e] + \int s^{(4)}e$ with $s^{(4)} = 0$.

Step 4: Boundary terms
$s'''$ is piecewise constant and $e(x_i) = 0$ at all nodes ⇒ the $s'''e$ terms vanish. $s''e'$ is continuous across the interior nodes: the sum telescopes to $s''(b)e'(b) - s''(a)e'(a) = 0$ because $s''(a) = s''(b) = 0$ (natural).

Step 5: Conclusion
So $\int s''e'' = 0$ and $\int(g'')^2 = \int(s'')^2 + \int(e'')^2 \ge \int(s'')^2$. Equality only for $e'' \equiv 0$, i.e. $e = 0$ ($e$ linear and $0$ at the nodes).

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
A Pythagoras-type theorem (orthogonality of $s''$ and $e''$) – orthogonality again, as in least squares (4.5).

exercises.title: Periodic spline
exercises.description: Determine the moments of the periodic cubic spline through the data $y = (0, 1, 0)$ with period $3$ (nodes $0, 1, 2$, $y_3 = y_0$, $h = 1$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The moment equations hold cyclically (indices modulo $3$): $M_{i-1} + 4M_i + M_{i+1} = 6(y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1})$.

Step 3: System
$\begin{pmatrix}4&1&1\\1&4&1\\1&1&4\end{pmatrix}M = \begin{pmatrix}6\\-12\\6\end{pmatrix}$ – cyclically tridiagonal.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Periodic: no boundary problem, but a cyclic system (solved with Sherman–Morrison, 4.3). The sum of the moments is $0$ here.

exercises.title: Uniqueness via diagonal dominance
exercises.description: Show that the moment system $\mathrm{tridiag}(1,4,1)$ is nonsingular for every size and estimate $\mathrm{cond}_\infty \le 3$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Strict diagonal dominance ⇒ nonsingular; for the inverse use the Neumann series or the dominance estimate.

Step 2: Nonsingularity
Row $i$: $|a_{ii}| = 4 > 2 \ge \sum_{j
e i}|a_{ij}|$. Suppose $Ax = 0$ with $x 
e 0$; let $|x_k| = \|x\|_\infty$. Row $k$: $4|x_k| \le |x_{k-1}| + |x_{k+1}| \le 2|x_k|$ – contradiction to $x_k 
e 0$.

Step 3: Bound for A⁻¹
The same computation for $Ax = b$: $4|x_k| \le |b_k| + 2|x_k|$, so $\|x\|_\infty \le \frac12\|b\|_\infty$ ⇒ $\|A^{-1}\|_\infty \le \frac12$.

Step 4: Condition
$\|A\|_\infty \le 6$, so $\mathrm{cond}_\infty(A) \le 6\cdot\frac12 = 3$ – independent of $n$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Spline interpolation is numerically a very benign problem – unlike polynomial interpolation with the Vandermonde matrix (4.9).

exercises.title: Justifying the O(h⁴) error order
exercises.description: Justify heuristically why the clamped cubic spline has error order $4$ and read the order off the table (errors $1.1\cdot10^{-3}$, $6.3\cdot10^{-5}$, $3.9\cdot10^{-6}$ for $n = 4, 8, 16$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The moments approximate $f''$ at the nodes; two integrations deliver the function.

Step 2: Moments
The moment equation is the central second difference $\frac{M_{i-1} + 4M_i + M_{i+1}}{6} = \frac{y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1}}{h^2}$; the right side is $f''(x_i) + \frac{h^2}{12}f^{(4)} + \dots$, the left one too ⇒ $M_i - f''(x_i) = O(h^2)$.

Step 3: Integration
$s'' - f''$ is $O(h^2)$. Integrating twice over an interval of length $h$ with zeros (interpolation conditions) gives $s - f = O(h^2\cdot h^2) = O(h^4)$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
For the natural spline $M_0 = 0$ interferes (if $f''(a) \ne 0$): only $O(h^2)$ there – hence clamped or not-a-knot for best results.

exercises.title: B-spline basis (idea)
exercises.description: The cubic B-spline $B(x)$ (support $[-2,2]$) has the values $B(0) = \frac23$, $B(\pm1) = \frac16$, $B(\pm2) = 0$ at the integers. Use this to show that the spline coefficient vector $c$ follows from $\mathrm{tridiag}(\frac16, \frac23, \frac16)c = y$ and explain the connection with the matrix $\mathrm{tridiag}(1,4,1)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Ansatz: $s(x) = \sum_jc_jB(x - j)$ – only three terms are nonzero at a node $x_i$.

Step 2: Interpolation
$s(i) = c_{i-1}B(1) + c_iB(0) + c_{i+1}B(-1) = \frac16c_{i-1} + \frac23c_i + \frac16c_{i+1} = y_i$.

Step 3: Connection
Multiplied by $6$: $c_{i-1} + 4c_i + c_{i+1} = 6y_i$ – the same matrix $\mathrm{tridiag}(1,4,1)$ as for the moments (here with data instead of second differences).

Step 4: Advantage
The basis functions $B(x - j)$ have local support: changing $c_j$ changes $s$ only on $[j - 2, j + 2]$. Difference from Lagrange polynomials (global).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
B-splines = standard basis in CAD (NURBS), computer graphics and statistics. Control points $c_j$ steer the curve locally.

exercises.title: Not-a-knot condition
exercises.description: For four points $(0,0), (1,1), (2,0), (3,1)$ the not-a-knot condition requires $s'''$ to be continuous at $x_1 = 1$ and $x_2 = 2$. Show that the spline is then the cubic interpolation polynomial and compare at $x = 0.5$ with the natural spline ($0.75$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Continuous third derivative at both interior nodes means: the same polynomial on all three pieces.

Step 2: Argument
Two neighbouring cubics with equal value, $s'$, $s''$ and $s'''$ at the node coincide as polynomials. So $s$ is a single polynomial of degree $\le 3$ through the 4 points – the interpolation polynomial.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
For few points the not-a-knot spline and the polynomial are identical; for many points not-a-knot acts only at the ends and is more accurate there than “natural”.

exercises.title: Checking a spline with a parameter for smoothness
exercises.description: For which $\alpha, \beta$ is $s(x) = x^3$ ($0 \le x \le 1$), $s(x) = 1 + \beta(x-1) + \alpha(x-1)^2$ ($1 \le x \le 2$) a $C^2$ spline? Is it then also $C^3$?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Compare values and derivatives at the node $x = 1$.

Step 2: Value
$s_0(1) = 1$, $s_1(1) = 1$ ✓ (independent of $\alpha, \beta$).

Step 5: C³?
$s_0''' = 6$, $s_1''' = 0$: jump. Not $C^3$ – but not required either. With an additional term $\gamma(x-1)^3$ we would have $s_1''' = 6\gamma$, and $\gamma = 1$ would give $s = x^3$ on $[0,2]$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
One parameter fewer per node: $C^2$ fixes $\alpha, \beta$, the third coefficient $\gamma$ stays free (that is the “jump in $s'''$”).
